6.191 Debugging Code Running in Containers
Line-by-line code debugging inside a container
Before we dive into this section about i d x _ d 9 7 e 5 c 1 5 debugging code running inside a container line by line, let me make a
disclaimer. What you will learn in this section should usually be your last resort if nothing else works. Ideally,
when following a test-driven approach when developing your application, the code is mostly guaranteed to work
since you have written unit and integration tests for it and run them against your code, which also runs in a
container. Alternatively, if unit or integration tests don't provide you with enough insight and you need to debug
your code line by line, you can do so by running your code directly on your host, thus leveraging the support of
development environments such as VS Code, Eclipse, or IntelliJ, to name just a few IDEs.
With all this preparation, you should rarely need to manually debug your code as it is running inside a container.
That said, let's see how you can do it!
In this section, we are going to concentrate exclusively on how to debug when using VS Code. Other editors and
IDEs may or may not offer similar capabilities.
Debugging a Node.js application
We'll start with the easiest i d x _ b 1 2 4 3 6 3 2 one – a Node.js application. We will use our sample application in the ~/The-Ultimate-
Docker-Container-Book-Fourth-Edition/chapter-06/solutions/node-sample folder, which we worked with
earlier in i d x _ e 9 6 0 5 8 a c this chapter:
Open a new terminal window i d x _ b a 7 c 9 8 b e and make sure that you navigate to this project folder:
$ cd ~/The-Ultimate-Docker-Container-Book-Fourth-Edition
$ cd chapter-06/node-sample
Open VS Code from within this container:
$ code .
In the terminal window, from within the project folder, run a container with our sample Node.js
application:
$ docker container run --rm -it --init \
--name node-demo \
-p 3000:3000 \
-p 9229:9229 \
-v $(pwd):/app \
node-demo-dev node --inspect=0.0.0.0 index.js

Instrumenting your code to produce meaningful logging
information
Once an application is running in i d x _ d b e 4 b 9 9 b production, it is impossible or strongly discouraged to interactively debug the
application. Thus, we need to come up with other ways to find the root cause when the system is behaving
unexpectedly or causing errors. The best way is to have the application generate detailed logging information that
can then be used by the developers that need to track down any errors. Since logging is such a common task, all
relevant programming languages or frameworks offer libraries that make the task i d x _ 1 b 2 0 6 6 7 3 of producing logging
information inside an application straightforward.
It is common to categorize the information that's output by an application as logs into so-called severity levels.

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: 11.12 199 Debugging Code Running in Containers
chunks.content:
11.12 199 Debugging Code Running in Containers
Here is a list of i d x _ f 5 0 2 c 3 3 5 those severity levels with a short description of each:
Log level Description

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: TRACE
chunks.content:
TRACE
Very fine-grained information. At this level, you are looking at capturing every detail
possible about your application's behavior.

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: DEBUG
chunks.content:
DEBUG
Relatively granular and mostly diagnostic information that helps you pin down potential
problems if they occur.

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: INFO
chunks.content:
INFO
Normal application behavior or milestones, such as startup or shutdown information.

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: WARNING
chunks.content:
WARNING
The application might have encountered a problem, or you detected an unusual situation.

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: ERROR
chunks.content:
ERROR
The application encountered a serious issue. This most probably represents the failure of an
important application task.

chunks.title: ultimatedockercontainerbookfourthedition
chunks.heading: FATAL
chunks.content:
FATAL
The catastrophic failure of your application. The immediate shutdown of the application is
advised.
Table 6.1 – A list of the severity levels used when generating logging information
Logging libraries usually allow a developer to define different log sinks – that is, destinations for the logging
information. Popular sinks are file sinks or a stream to the console. When working with containerized applications,
it is strongly recommended that you always direct logging output to the console or STDOUT. Docker will then make
this information available to you via the docker container logs command. Other log collectors, such as Logstash,
Fluentd, Loki, and others, can also be used to scrape this information.

Chapter 6 204
Now that we have learned how to instrument code to simplify how we can find the root cause of an issue when
running in production, next, we will look at how we can instrument a distributed application using the
OpenTracing standard for distributed tracing and then use Jaeger as a tool.
Using OpenTelemetry and Jaeger to monitor and
troubleshoot
When we want to monitor and troubleshoot i d x _ 0 0 8 a 6 5 5 d transactions in a complex distributed system, we need something a
bit more powerful than what we have just learned. Of course, we can and should continue to instrument our code
with meaningful logging messages, yet we need something more on top of that. This something more is the
capability i d x _ 7 7 4 8 e b 7 9 to trace a single request or transaction end to end, as it flows through a system consisting of many
application services. Ideally, we also want to capture other interesting metrics, such as the time spent on each
component versus the total time that the request took.
Luckily, we do not have to reinvent the wheel. There is battle-tested open source software out there that helps us
achieve the aforementioned goals. Two examples of such infrastructure components or software are i d x _ 5 1 b 3 c 3 1 6
OpenTelemetry (https://opentelemetry.io/) and i d x _ f d d 7 b e d b Jaeger (https://www.jaegertracing.io/). When using Jaeger,
you run a central Jaeger server component, and each application component uses a Jaeger client that will forward
debug and tracing information transparently to the Jaeger server component. There are Jaeger clients for all major
programming languages i d x _ 1 e 2 2 d a f c and frameworks, such as Node.js, Python, Java, and .NET.
We will not go into all the intimate details of how to use Jaeger in this book, but we will provide a high-level
overview of how it works conceptually.
Instrumenting a .NET application
In this section, we're going to i d x _ d f c e 2 f a 8 show how to instrument a .NET application. Please follow the following i d x _ 0 e a 9 d 1 1 8 instruction
to do so:

$ dotnet add package OpenTelemetry.Extensions.Hosting
$ dotnet add package \
OpenTelemetry.Instrumentation.AspNetCore \
$ dotnet add package \
OpenTelemetry.Instrumentation.Http
$ dotnet add package \
OpenTelemetry.Exporter.OpenTelemetryProtocol
$ dotnet add package OpenTelemetry.Exporter.Console

chunks.content:
Chapter 6 212
Summary
In this chapter, you discover how to reshape container-based development into a fluid, responsive workflow that
rivals local environments. By bind-mounting your host code into the container with Docker's --volume flag, you
see every save instantly without rebuilding images. Coupled with language-specific watch tools – nodemon for
Node.js, Spring Boot DevTools, Flask's reloader (or nodemon --exec python), and .NET's dotnet watch run tool –
you eliminate manual restarts entirely. You also learn to attach debuggers seamlessly by exposing the appropriate
ports (for example, 9229 for Node.js) and adding flags (--inspect=0.0.0.0), enabling full breakpoints, stepping,
and variable inspection exactly as you would in a local IDE session.
Beyond swift iteration and in-container debugging, the chapter emphasizes robust observability: writing
structured log messages to STDOUT / STDERR ensures Docker's logging driver captures every event, viewable via
docker container logs or integrated logging backends. Finally, by instrumenting services with OpenTracing
standard and running Jaeger's all-in-one Docker image, you gain distributed, end-to-end tracing – visualizing
request flows, pinpointing latency hotspots, and inspecting custom spans and tags. Together, these patterns
empower you to develop, debug, and troubleshoot containerized applications with maximum productivity and
minimal friction.
In the next chapter, we are going to show you how using Docker containers can supercharge your automation,
from running a simple automation task in a container to using containers to build a CI/CD pipeline.
Questions
Please try to answer the following questions covering key concepts and hands-on skills described in the chapter to
assess your learning progress:
What docker run option allows you to map your local source folder into a container so that code changes
on the host appear inside the running container immediately?
After volume-mapping your source folder into a running container, you modify and save a file. Why
won't your application pick up the change automatically, and what two manual steps must you perform
to see the update?
In a Node.js development image, which tool can you install and invoke instead of node index.js to
restart the app automatically on code changes? How do you modify your Dockerfile to use it?
Which dependency must you add to a Spring Boot project's pom.xml file (or build.gradle) to enable
automatic restart on code changes when running in a container?
What two approaches were shown for auto-restarting a Flask-based Python app on code change within a
container?
Which dotnet command replaces dotnet run to watch for file changes and hot-reload a .NET app inside
a container?
When and why would you debug code line by line when running inside a container?
